steps.body: The exact same division can demand three different answers, depending on the story. **Round UP** when leftovers still need a whole extra unit (one more van for the extra kids). **Round DOWN** when leftovers can't form another whole group (extra players don't make a full team). **Split as a fraction** when you're sharing something that CAN be cut, like food. The math is identical — the story picks the ending.
Sort each story by its ending.

widget.prompt: Sort each story by how its remainder should be handled.

items.label: 51 kids, 8 per van — how many vans are needed?
items.feedback: 51 ÷ 8 = 6 remainder 3 — the 3 leftover kids still need a whole extra van: 7 vans.

items.label: 43 books, 6 per box — how many boxes are needed?
items.feedback: 43 ÷ 6 = 7 remainder 1 — that one leftover book still needs a box: 8 boxes.

items.label: 38 kids, teams of 5 — how many FULL teams can be made?
items.feedback: 38 ÷ 5 = 7 remainder 3 — the 3 leftover kids can't form a full team, so just 7 teams.

items.label: 50 eggs, dozens of 12 — how many FULL dozens?
items.feedback: 50 ÷ 12 = 4 remainder 2 — the 2 leftover eggs don't make a dozen, so just 4 dozens.

items.label: 9 sandwiches shared equally among 4 friends
items.feedback: 9 ÷ 4 = 2 remainder 1 — sandwiches can be cut, so each friend gets 2 whole plus 1/4 more.

items.label: 7 chocolate bars shared equally between 2 friends
items.feedback: 7 ÷ 2 = 3 remainder 1 — bars can be cut, so each friend gets 3 whole plus 1/2 more.

widget.missFeedback: Ask: does the leftover need a whole extra container (up), get dropped as too few for a group (down), or get physically cut (fraction)?
widget.successFeedback: Needing enough containers rounds up; counting only complete groups rounds down; cuttable shares become fractions.

predict.prompt: 27 kids, and each car holds 4. Does the remainder mean you SKIP a car or ADD one?
predict.reveal: Three leftover kids still need seats — the context rounds UP. The same remainder gets dropped, rounded, or reported depending on what the story demands.

explanationVariants: 34 ÷ 6 = 5 remainder 4 — the 4 leftover people still need a boat, so it takes 6 trips, not 5.
Rounding up from 5 remainder 4 gives 6 — the leftover people can't be left behind.

widget.prompt: A boat holds 6 people; 34 people need to cross. How many boat trips are needed?

options.label: 6 trips — the leftover 4 people still need a trip
options.feedback: 34 ÷ 6 = 5 remainder 4; those 4 people can't be left on shore, so it's 6 trips.

options.label: 5 trips — that's the quotient
options.feedback: 5 trips only moves 30 people. The last 4 still need to cross — round up to 6 trips.

options.label: 34 trips — one per person
options.feedback: The boat carries 6 at once, not 1. 34 ÷ 6 = 5 remainder 4, rounded up to 6 trips.

options.label: 4 trips — that's the remainder
options.feedback: 4 is just the leftover people, not the trip count. The full answer rounds the quotient up: 6 trips.

steps.body: The fraction ending turns the remainder into a piece of the whole: **remainder ⁄ divisor.** For 9 sandwiches among 4 friends: 9 ÷ 4 = 2 remainder 1, and that leftover 1 sandwich splits into fourths — each friend's fair share is 2 and 1/4 sandwiches (2¼). The remainder becomes the fraction's numerator; the divisor becomes its denominator.

explanationVariants: 11 ÷ 4 = 2 remainder 3, and that leftover 3 splits into fourths: each friend gets 2 and 3/4.
The remainder (3) becomes the numerator over the divisor (4): 3/4 more, plus the whole 2.

widget.prompt: 11 cookies shared equally among 4 kids (cookies can be broken). Each kid gets 2 whole cookies, plus a fraction. What is the NUMERATOR of that fraction (over 4)?

commonErrors.feedback: 2 is the whole-cookie count each kid gets. The fraction's numerator is the LEFTOVER after that: 11 − (4×2) = 3.
4 is the denominator (how many kids share each broken cookie), not the numerator. The numerator is the remainder: 3.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Find the remainder of 11 ÷ 4 — that's the fraction's numerator.

steps.body: Match the question type to its rule.

widget.prompt: Match each question style to the rule it follows.

left.label: "How many are NEEDED to fit everyone?"
"How many COMPLETE groups can be made?"
"How much does each person get, sharing equally?"

right.label: Round UP — the leftover still needs a spot
Round DOWN — the leftover can't form a full group
Fraction — the leftover gets cut and shared

pairErrors.feedback: 'Complete groups' asks what's fully finished — leftovers that can't fill another group get dropped, not rounded up.

widget.missFeedback: 'Needed to fit' rounds up; 'complete groups' rounds down; 'share equally' becomes a fraction.
widget.successFeedback: Three question styles, three endings — the words in the story are the clue every time.

explanationVariants: 112 ÷ 15 = 7 remainder 7 — the 7 leftover chairs still need a row, so 8 rows are needed to fit them all.
Rounding up from 7 remainder 7 gives 8 rows.

widget.prompt: 112 chairs need to be set up; each row holds 15 chairs. How many rows are needed to fit them ALL?

commonErrors.feedback: 7 rows only fits 105 chairs (7 × 15). The last 7 chairs still need a row — round up to 8.
15 is chairs per row, not a row count. 112 ÷ 15 = 7 remainder 7, rounded up to 8 rows.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Divide 112 by 15; if there's any remainder, round the quotient up.

hints: Divide 89 by 20 to find the quotient and remainder.
4 buses carry 80 students (20 × 4) — 9 students are still waiting.
Those 9 leftover students still need a bus.
explanationVariants: 89 ÷ 20 = 4 remainder 9 — the 9 leftover students still need a bus, so 5 buses are needed so nobody is left behind.
Rounding up from 4 remainder 9 gives 5 buses.

widget.prompt: 89 students are going on a field trip. Each bus seats 20 students. How many buses are needed so nobody is left behind?

commonErrors.feedback: 4 buses only seats 80 students (4 × 20). The 9 students still waiting need a bus too — round up to 5.
9 is the leftover student count, not the bus count. Round the quotient up instead: 4 becomes 5.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Divide 89 by 20; since there's a remainder, round the quotient up.

takeaways: Round UP when the leftover still needs a whole extra unit.
Round DOWN when the leftover can't fill one more full group.
Split as a fraction (remainder over divisor) when the leftover can be physically shared.

concept.body: Quick rewind. Ask what the leftover people or things actually NEED. If they still need a spot (a seat, a container), **round up.** If the story only counts finished, complete groups, **round down** and drop the leftover. Reading the question's exact words is the whole trick.

explanationVariants: 23 ÷ 5 = 4 remainder 3 — the 3 leftover kids still need a pencil pack, so 5 packs are needed.
Rounding up from 4 remainder 3 gives 5 packs.

widget.prompt: 23 kids each need a pencil; pencils come in packs of 5. How many packs are needed so every kid gets one?

options.label: 5 packs
options.feedback: 23 ÷ 5 = 4 remainder 3 — those 3 kids still need a pack, so round up to 5.

options.label: 4 packs
options.feedback: 4 packs gives pencils to only 20 kids. The 3 left over still need one — round up to 5.

options.label: 3 packs
options.feedback: 3 is the leftover kid count, not the pack count. Rounding the quotient (4) up gives 5 packs.
